extracted.intended_audience: educators, educational theorists, policymakers, and students of education
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical principles for organizing education in a democratic society, addressing the relation of liberal (intellectual) and mechanical (utilitarian) studies, the role of experience vs. knowledge, and curricular aims to unify culture and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between mechanical and liberal education
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of education correspond to servile and free activities: the base or mechanical trains by practical exercises for capacity in doing things (habituation and technical skill), while the liberal or intellectual aims to train intelligence for its proper office: to know. The less knowledge has to do with practical affairs, the more adequately it engages intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical training operates through repetition and assiduity in application; liberal education emphasizes awakening and nurturing thought. Example: practice in playing instruments is tolerated only insofar as it conduces to appreciation; if professional power is aimed at, the practice sinks from the liberal to the professional level (Aristotle's point that one might as well teach cooking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal education as knowing for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the education that makes for power to know as an end in itself, without reference to the practice of even civic duties, is truly liberal or free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A purely intellectual life is self-sufficing; knowing for the sake of knowing is independent. Civic activities retain some taint of practice and dependence upon others; true liberal education makes reason an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile culture and utility in curriculum design
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture (liberal education) and utility (practical training) need not be hostile; education should construct courses of study that are useful and liberal at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the inorganic composite where cultural subjects are socially useless and utilitarian subjects fail to liberate imagination. Analyze meanings of both culture and utility to build unity rather than compromise. Example: natural science should be tied to application rather than taught as isolated accomplishment; music/literature should not be reduced to technical skill alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid training that renders persons unfit for exercise of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: An occupation deserves to be called mechanical if it renders the body, soul, or intellect of free persons unfit for the exercise and practice of excellence; mercenary employments or those degrading the body are mechanical insofar as they deprive the intellect of leisure and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If gainful pursuits deprive the intellect of the conditions for its exercise (leisure, dignity), they should be regarded as mechanical and their associated training as illiberal. The standard is the extent to which work allows intellectual exercise and self-sufficing activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as an instrument of democratic emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational transformation is needed to give full and explicit effect to social changes toward democracy so that all share in useful service and enjoy a worthy leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to replace educational segregation (culture vs utility) with measures that make thought a guide of free practice for all and make leisure a reward of accepting responsibility for service rather than exemption from it. This requires reorganizing curricula and school systems (common, public, free education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction aiming at utilitarian results must not sacrifice cultural faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where instruction in aiming at utilitarian results sacrifices imagination, the refining of taste, and the deepening of intellectual insight (cultural values), it also, to the same degree, renders what is learned limited in its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrow modes of skill (mere habit) cannot be made useful beyond themselves; skills achieved with deepening knowledge and judgment transfer readily to new situations. Avoid teaching that reduces study to rote drill at the expense of judgment and imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare workers intellectually, not merely with rudimentary skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Education for those who work should go beyond a few years devoted to rudimentary symbols (reading, writing, arithmetic) and include training in science, literature, and history so workers can take advantage of mechanization and have intellectual engagement with their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanization can free the mind for higher thought only if workers are prepared with broader intellectual resources; narrow early schooling fails to equip workers to utilize leisure or intellectual opportunities created by technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster active participation in ends that control activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Work becomes free or voluntary when men have an active concern in the ends that control their activity; education should cultivate direct participation and concern so action is not merely for the employer's ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political democracy provides mechanisms for participation; economic relations often remain autocratic. Education that unifies disposition and fosters concern for social aims helps render work voluntary and less servile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid isolating 'object lessons' and pure sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalistic empiricism and object lessons that isolate sense-activity tend to reduce instruction to a 'physical gymnastic' of sense-organs and neglect the role of thinking; the sensory impression alone is an inadequate basis for constructive education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While firsthand acquaintance with objects is valuable, treating sensations as ends leads to fragmentation and neglect of judgment, comparison, and the constructive building of meanings. Object lessons should be integrated with reflective thought rather than used as isolated sensory units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must be constructive, not merely critical (critique of sensationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalism served a critical role in dissolving dogma, but as a theory of education it is weak on the constructive side: education requires building up new experience into intellectual habitudes rather than only destroying false beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensationalist emphasis on reception of impressions undervalues active mental operations necessary for forming stable, organized knowledge. Dewey notes at least three defects of sensationalistic empiricism, beginning with its insufficient constructive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach present subject matter as intrinsically significant, not merely as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should emphasize present literary and intellectual content possessed of aesthetic and moral significance rather than treating studies merely as instruments for later use (e.g., not teaching reading/writing/arithmetic solely as tools to 'get ahead').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek schooling modeled this by subordinating acquisition of skill to literary content; modern elementary motives that treat school studies entirely as means to employment encourage drill and automatic skill rather than present intellectual engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor skills developed with understanding and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Skills that are achieved alongside deepening of knowledge and perfection of judgment are flexible and controllable by the individual; such skills are genuinely useful across situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with rule-of-thumb or routine skills: the empiricist/trial-and-error mode leads to narrow applicability. Curriculum should aim for transferability by embedding skills in principles and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of historical/social origins of educational dualism
rubrics_metrics.description: The split between culture and utility is historical and social (originating in Greece and linked to class divisions), not an intrinsic natural necessity; recognizing this helps target educational reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding that educational distinctions grew from social arrangements (leisure vs labor, learned vs unlearned) shows that reform of social and educational practices (not merely theoretical redefinition) is necessary to overcome dualism.
